description: We are a five-member Egyptian team from Ismailia STEM High School, bringing together diverse skills in softwarment, research, game design, and storytelling. Based across Port Said and Cairo, we share a passion for making space exploration and scientific knowledge more accessible through interactive, story-driven experiences.
summary: Last Hope Project Solution Last Hope is an educational 2D web based space archaeology and survival game designed to teach players how aerospace engineering, robotics, and planetary science work by turning real NASA mission data and historical Mars hardware into an interactive, story driven adventure. Players step into the role of a remote rover operator in the year 2326, travel across authentic Martian regions, inspect abandoned spacecraft, and use hands on engineering mini games to solve historical mission anomalies, making space science both fun and accessible for learners everywhere.
details:
Last Hope is an educational 2D, overhead-view web game about recovering lost engineering knowledge on Mars. In the year 2326, players take the role of an agent controlling a robot sent to Mars by ARES (Agency for the Recovery of Exploration Science), a global organization formed after nuclear wars destroyed humanity’s modern technology. Players explore Mars-themed environments, discover four forgotten NASA artifacts, learn why each one failed, and solve a puzzle for each. Everything they learn is then used to build the one tool that can bring the robot and its data home.

Solution

In the year 2326, about three centuries after nuclear wars destroyed all of humanity’s modern technology, nearly all knowledge remains locked inside digital devices that have become artifacts people scavenge for. As humanity slowly recovered the lost knowledge, advanced nations became interested in exploring space and formed ARES. ARES sent a robot to Mars on a space shuttle, and the player is the agent responsible for controlling it and keeping it safe. Because the robot’s technology is based on old algorithms and techniques, it can only survive outside the shuttle for a limited time, or it will be destroyed. Meanwhile, the shuttle’s external propulsion-control connection was damaged on arrival, so it cannot safely start its return journey. The player must craft a Robotic Spacecraft Repair Arm (RSRA) to fix it, which costs 45 Points of Knowledge (POK). The player earns POK by discovering and solving the puzzles of four forgotten NASA artifacts.

Gameplay Flow

After a short opening scene, the player enters their age and name. A map button guides them to each artifact. Each artifact first shows basic information on the map (timeline, description, location). After the player discovers it, the game explains why it failed. Solving its puzzle reveals one way the problem could be overcome. A discoveries panel shows six circles: the four NASA artifacts, Tarsy, and a final “Coming soon” circle marked “????” to build anticipation. Each circle shows a picture once the item is partially discovered (found on the map) or fully discovered (puzzle solved), and “???” before that.

Missions

Tarsy (Tutorial)

• The first discovery is Tarsy, a broken robot described as an “old civilization robot that might be handy in some way.” Tarsy is not an official NASA artifact. It is a tool from our imagination, added to keep players engaged.

• Players repair Tarsy with a simple puzzle: connecting the red wire to the blue wire by dragging.

• Once repaired, Tarsy follows the player, gives hints, and carries the tools the player may need: a lock cutter, a LASER, a scanner, and Shuffle. It can also point out where the next artifact is.

• Repairing Tarsy earns 5 POK, unlocks the next artifact on the map, and adds the POK counter and the Craft button to the interface.

HP3 Mole (Elysium Planitia)

• The HP3 Mole was a self-hammering thermal probe designed to burrow 3 to 5 meters underground and measure Mars’s internal heat flow. It landed in 2018, was deployed in 2019, and its final penetration attempt concluded in 2021.

• Why it failed: insufficient soil friction. The probe met cohesive duricrust instead of loose soil, which made it bounce in place.

• Puzzle: the game explains that the friction between the soil and the digger must increase, and shows “Pushing Force Value = 1.” The player chooses a replacement value from 0.5, 1, or 5. The correct answer is 5. If the player is stuck, Tarsy’s hint is that they need a value bigger than 1.

• How to overcome it: recoil suppression, an expandable anchoring collar, and robotic-arm-assisted rotary-percussive drilling.

Viking 1 Seismometer (Chryse Planitia)

• This three-axis seismic instrument landed in July 1976 to detect Martian ground vibrations.

• Why it failed: its uncaging mechanism failed. The release pins did not fire, which kept the internal sensors permanently locked.

• Puzzle: the caging mechanism is broken, and the player must free the sensor by removing the locking bar and pin at the top right. Using the LASER, which the player drags with the cursor, they cut the locking bar and open the cage.

• How to overcome it: a lock-free sensor architecture, redundant release actuators, and thermally matched low-expansion materials.

Ingenuity Mars Helicopter (Jezero Crater)

• Ingenuity was a lightweight, autonomous coaxial helicopter technology demonstrator. Its first flight was in April 2021 and its final flight in January 2024.

• Why it failed: navigation tracking loss. Its downward camera lost tracking over featureless sand ripples, which led to a hard landing and damaged rotor blades.

• Puzzle: Tarsy investigates and explains the cause, then says the helicopter can’t be repaired but can still be useful. The player extracts the camera from the wreck, and the helicopter is then shown with the camera.

• How to overcome it: multi-sensor fusion (stereo cameras, an IMU, and altimeters) and rotor blades reinforced with tougher polymer composites.

Viking 1 Surface Sampler Arm (Chryse Planitia)

• This extendible robotic boom with a collector scoop landed in July 1976 to dig soil.

• Why it failed: a mechanical jam. The boom latch pin failed to drop free during the initial extension and obstructed the arm, though the arm was later recovered.

• Puzzle: the player investigates the arm, finds that the boom did not extend far enough to release the pin, and understands how this jammed the mechanism. They then recreate NASA’s historical recovery by extending the boom further until the pin is released. The hint is to pull the boom to a distinct point to finish it.

• How to overcome it: spring-assisted self-releasing latches and extension verification sensors.

Crafting the RSRA and the Ending

Each of the four artifacts gives 10 POK (5 for discovering it and 5 for solving its puzzle), and repairing Tarsy adds 5 more, for exactly the 45 POK the Craft button requires. In the craft machine, the knowledge from each artifact becomes one component. The player must drag the four components into their correct positions.

• Base Clamp: the anchoring mechanism (HP3 Mole solution).

• Release Unit: the locking mechanism (Viking 1 Seismometer).

• Sensor Head: the camera and motion sensors (Ingenuity).

• Telescopic Arm: the extension mechanism and gripper (Viking 1 Surface Sampler Arm).

The arm is inspired by NASA’s Canadarm. Once assembled, it anchors itself to the shuttle and automatically fixes the damaged connection. In the ending scene, the robot, damaged internally and close to the end of its operating time, reaches the shuttle at the last minute. The shuttle returns to Earth carrying the data needed to recover the lost technology, and everyone celebrates. The closing text reads: “Congratulations on discovering the lost pieces. What you have accomplished will never be forgotten. Simply because, you returned the LAST HOPE to humanity at the LAST MINUTE.”

The Game Benefits

Students, educators, gamers, and the wider community benefit by:

• Teaching real NASA Mars mission history, including why each instrument failed and how engineers could overcome those failures.

• Encouraging problem solving through simple, hands-on puzzles (dragging wires, choosing values, using a laser, extending a boom, extracting a camera, assembling a tool).

• Bridging the gap between open mission archives from NASA and modern interactive storytelling in a fun, accessible, browser-based experience.

• Encouraging systems thinking, spatial reasoning, and scientific curiosity among learners without requiring prior engineering training or expensive hardware.

Our Goal

To make open mission data and engineering history from NASA more accessible, helping communities reconnect with space exploration while addressing declining student engagement in STEM fields (highlighted by 2024 NAEP science metrics) and narrowing public awareness of space milestones (reflected in 2023 Pew Research data). Despite our effort to showcase authentic planetary exploration and historical problem solving, our Season 1 campaign is focused on four iconic Mars surface missions and does not yet include orbital spacecraft, lunar landers, or outer planet probes. The “Coming soon” slot points to future content, and future expansions can integrate additional planetary bodies, cooperative classroom challenges, and expanded datasets to broaden global scientific literacy.

Tools and Technologies Used

Game Engine, Coding Languages, and Web Architecture

• KAPLAY (JavaScript/TypeScript) is our core game engine for the 2D top-down game. We use its built-in component system, with the area() and pos() components on physical entities and body({ isStatic: true }) on walls and solid objects, so the engine handles collision and boundaries natively. Interactions use KAPLAY’s onUpdate() and onCollide() methods.

• JavaScript (ES6) powers top-down robot navigation, interactive puzzle workspaces, and drag-and-drop interactions.

• HTML DOM overlay handles the user interface. Health, inventory, labels, scores, and menus are standard HTML elements positioned absolutely over the game canvas, and the JavaScript game loop updates them with document.getElementById().

• HTML5 and CSS3 structure the responsive web layouts and cross-platform browser compatibility, and style the overlay with Flexbox and Grid, giving the game a cohesive post-apocalyptic Martian orange-to-brown visual aesthetic.

• JSON is used to structure historical mission timelines, artifact information, and educational field notes across every stage of the campaign.

Data Sources

• Open Mission Archives and Telemetry Datasets from NASA provide authentic Martian terrain coordinates (Elysium Planitia, Chryse Planitia, and Jezero Crater), spacecraft hardware specifications, and real anomaly parameters.

• Through open repositories provided by NASA, we accessed landing site telemetry, regolith density profiles, and engineering failure reports that allowed us to model authentic spacecraft challenges and compare real mission constraints with the solutions players work through.

• Historical mission information from InSight (HP3 Mole), Viking 1, and Ingenuity was used to write each artifact’s description, failure explanation, and recovery solution.

Visual and Interface Design

• Custom Vector and Sprite Assets bring to life the top-down Mars-themed maps, the robot and Tarsy sprites, environmental landmarks, and interactive puzzle visuals.

• Our interface was recreated in the style of our UI mock-ups.

• Lastica and Clean Sans Serif Typography establish a clear visual hierarchy and high-contrast legibility during puzzles.

Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

We used AI tools as a supportive resource throughout the project. Specifically:

• Design: When brainstorming creative design ideas, we used AI to explore ways to translate real spacecraft engineering anomalies into intuitive, tactile 2D puzzle mechanics.

• Implementation Guidance: When structuring specific features, we prompted AI for modular JavaScript state management, canvas rendering loops, and responsive CSS Grid and Flexbox best practices.

• Debugging Assistance: During development, AI was used to help identify, explain, and resolve logic errors in puzzle physics calculations, collision boundaries, and UI interactions.

• Content Refinement: AI assisted in reviewing mission logs and educational summaries to maintain clarity, consistency, and scientific accuracy.

Design Considerations and Scientific Rigor

Throughout development, our team carefully balanced scientific fidelity with intuitive gameplay so players experience authentic engineering principles without feeling overwhelmed by technical jargon. By pairing clear visuals, short puzzles, and progressive hints from Tarsy with a responsive zero-install browser architecture, Last Hope ensures that students, educators, science centers, and curious minds anywhere in the world can engage meaningfully with real space exploration history and technical discovery across diverse educational environments.
